title: 5 Theses Against AI Humanoid Teachers
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Prompted by a New York school district's plan to deploy a humanoid AI robot as a classroom aide, Matthews lays out five theses against putting humanoid robots in classrooms, writing explicitly from a Christian worldview while noting the argument doesn't depend on it. His first thesis holds that the human/robot distinction is developmentally crucial and that placing a human-looking, human-sounding robot in a classroom gives young learners the poorest possible preparation for keeping that distinction clear. His second reframes AI's proper role: efficiency gained from AI should be reinvested in human connection, not used to replace it. His third thesis argues education requires more than knowledge transfer because students are 'heart-soul-mind-strength' persons, not merely brains to be filled with facts, so a robot cannot fulfill education's full purpose even in principle. The fourth thesis warns that AI teacher aides are a functional first step toward AI teachers regardless of how the technology is marketed, and the fifth cites a Cohen and Riel study on writing audience to argue that work reviewed only by an AI-graded audience will devastate student motivation. Matthews notes in an edit that the specific New York district's plans have been paused, but frames this as a temporary reprieve rather than a resolved question.
points: Thesis 1: placing a human-looking, human-sounding robot in a classroom clouds the crucial robot/human distinction for young learners at exactly the age they most need it kept clear.

Thesis 2 reframes AI's proper role in teaching: efficiency gained through AI should fund more time for parent communication, colleague conversation, and 1-1 student work -- connection is what matters most, not what should be sped up.

Thesis 3 draws on theologian Andy Crouch's framing of humans as 'heart-soul-mind-strength complexes designed for love,' arguing education requires a whole person to educate a whole person, not a knowledge-delivery system.

Thesis 4 is explicitly a slippery-slope argument: Matthews maps a step-by-step progression from a small AI-aide pilot to 'robots now teach our sons and daughters,' arguing there are no brakes on this train.

Thesis 5 cites a Cohen and Riel study finding students wrote better essays for peer audiences than for teacher-graded ones, and asks how much less motivating writing becomes when the only audience is an algorithmically-powered humanoid.
quotes: If an impressionable young learner shares a classroom with a human looking, human sounding, and human feeling robot, we're giving them the poorest possible preparation for keeping the robot/human distinction clear in their minds.
Relating to students isn't something we outsource to make room for other things, it's the thing we make room for.

Theologian Andy Crouch argues we are "heart-soul-mind-strength complexes designed for love." You may or may not agree with his Christian perspective, but I hope it prompts you to see that treating learners as merely brains to be filled with facts is a mistake.
There is a clear and obvious line from AI teacher aides to AI teachers, and to encourage the former is to pave the way for the latter.

A seminal study by Cohen and Riel found that students writing for peers wrote better essays than when writing for teachers for a semester grade. It mattered to the students that someone would not just read, but desire to read their work.
Five theses, one big idea: humans should be educated by humans.
